narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Second, your first-year ranking was almost equally damaging; you also placed in the lowest decile, far below the average of 6 among students who were accepted. These two early academic signals outweighed everything else in the model’s eyes.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.20 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward success. Unfortunately, this positive nudge was not nearly enough to overcome the impact of your low class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 35, middle family income, full-time status, gender, and race played much smaller roles and did not meaningfully change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and class standing in the coming year. Stronger grades and a higher class rank in your final year could substantially lower your predicted risk of failing the bar exam and open doors to admission in future application cycles.
